blocks.text: Snake Bites

A snakebite can be life-threatening if the snake is venomous. Less than 10% of 3500 snake species are venomous and they include different species of Cobras, Mambas and Adders which are endemic in Tanzania. Clinical Presentation of a snakebite varies depending on the type of envenomation a snake causes. The severity of the symptoms depends on the amount of venom the snake injects into the victim. Some snakebites (10-30%) can be considered as dry bites where no venom is injected. As a late appearance if symptoms after a snakebite is possible up to 24 hours a close monitoring needs to be conducted in this time frame.

blocks.text: Types of Envenomation are:
Neurotoxic Envenomation: in non-spitting cobras, mambas and sea snakes
Hemotoxic Envenomation: in vipers, boomslang and Vine Snake
Cytotoxic Envenomation: in Puffadder, Gaboon Adder, Night Adder, Stiletto Snake and Spitting Cobras
Mixed Cytotoxic and Hemotoxic Envenomation: in Spitting Cobras and Puff Adder

A snakebite should be considered in any patient, presenting with severe pain or swelling of a limb or in any unexplained illness presenting with bleeding or abnormal neurological signs. Some cobras spit venom into the eyes of victims causing pain and inflammation.

Reassure the patient and try to calm the patient down.
Immobilize the extremity where the patient was bitten to reduce the spread and absorption of venom, Use a Splint or Pressure Immobilization Bandage.

blocks.text: Supportive Treatments may be required and include intubation & ventilation in neurotoxic snakebite patients, wound debridement in cytotoxic snakebite patients and blood transfusion in hemotoxic snakebite cases.

runs.text: Supportive Treatments may be required and include intubation & ventilation in neurotoxic snakebite patients, wound debridement in cytotoxic snakebite patients and blood transfusion in hemotoxic snakebite cases.

blocks.text: Symptoms might last for days and require permanent monitoring.
Do endotracheal intubation +/- elective tracheotomy if respiratory distress due to weakness occurs.
Monitor the patient closely for a minimum time of 24 hours after the snakebite. Symptoms can appear late, and envenomation can progress rapidly.
Surgical Intervention:
Dead tissue should be removed from the wound.
If there are signs of compartment syndrome a surgical intervention is required. Incisions to relieve pressure in the limb might be required.

runs.text: If there are signs of compartment syndrome a surgical intervention is required. Incisions to relieve pressure in the limb might be required.

blocks.text: Skin grafting, if there is an extensive necrosis present.
Tracheotomy if paralysis of muscles involved in swallowing occurs.
Pharmacological Management
Fluid resuscitation for patients in shock
A: sodium chloride 0.9% (IV) 10-20ml/kg. Repeat the dose after 30 minutes if shock is still present. Use Vasopressors if the shock is persistent. Keep monitoring the Fluid intake and output.

Provide ventilatory support if respiratory paralysis develops.

Adverse reaction due to Polyvalent Snake Antivenom

In case of Polyvalent Snake Antivenom administration mild anaphylaxis can occur in around 20-30% of the cases and severe anaphylaxis can occur in around 5-10% of the cases. Other than that, serum sickness, a late reaction to the Polyvalent Snake Antivenom can occur 7-21 days after the administration. Anaphylaxis is treated with Epinephrine (adrenaline) (IM).

runs.text: Snake Antivenom can occur 7-21 days after the administration.

blocks.text: A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (IM) dose of 1:1000 (Repeat after 3-5 minutes if no improvement)
Children < 6 years old: 150mcg IM (0,15ml)
Children 6-12 years old: 300mcg IM (0,3ml)
Children > 12 years old & Adults 500mcg IM (0,5ml)
AND
A: chlorpheniramine (PO) (be ready if allergic reaction occurs). Dosage as below
Children under 6years: 4mg 8hourly as needed
6–12 years: 8mg 12hourly as needed.
>12 years and older 12mg 12hourly as needed
Note:
If itching/rash, restlessness, cough, respiratory distress or hypotension develops stop Polyvalent Snake Antivenom and give:
A: epinephrine (adrenaline) (SC) 0.01 ml/kg of 1/1000 or 0.1 ml/kg of 1/10,000 solution
AND
A: chlorpheniramine (IM/ IV/SC) 250 micrograms/kg.
When the patient is stable restart the Polyvalent Snake Antivenom infusion.
Antivenom can be given every two hours until the patient’s condition improves, or the progression of the symptoms has stopped.
Blood transfusion may be required if HB drops < 7mg/dl.
Serum sickness usually occurs within 7-21 days and is treated with Steroids.
Response of abnormal neurological signs to antivenom is more variable and depends on type of venom.
